debit spread.def: A spread of options bought for a net payment. The most it can lose is that payment.

credit spread.def: A spread of options sold for a net receipt, which is the most it can make. The bought option or options cap its loss.

call debit spread.def: A position that buys a call and sells a call with a higher strike on the same underlying and expiry, for a net payment. It profits if the underlying rises, with both its gain and its loss capped. Also called a bull call spread or a long call spread.

put debit spread.def: A position that buys a put and sells a put with a lower strike on the same underlying and expiry, for a net payment. It profits if the underlying falls, with both its gain and its loss capped. Also called a bear put spread or a long put spread.

iron butterfly.def: A four-option position that sells a put and a call at the same strike and buys a put below and a call above it as wings. It profits most if the underlying finishes at the middle strike, and the wings cap its loss.

poor man's covered call.def: A diagonal call spread that buys a deep in-the-money call with a distant expiry, often a LEAPS call, in place of shares, and sells shorter-dated out-of-the-money calls against it. Abbreviated PMCC.

ratio backspread.def: A position that sells one option and buys more options of the same type further out of the money, often for little or no net premium. The call version profits most from a strong rally, the put version from a crash.

IV crush.def: The fall in implied volatility once an awaited event, such as an earnings report, has passed. It cuts the value of options bought before the event, even when the price moves the way their buyer expected.

protective put.def: A position that holds shares and buys a put below their price, so that the put caps the loss on the shares in exchange for its premium.

wing.def: One of the bought options at the outside strikes of a spread, condor or butterfly, which caps the position's loss on that side. The width of a wing is the distance from the sold strike to the bought one beyond it.

butterfly spread.def: A three-strike position, all calls or all puts, that buys one option at each outer strike and sells two at the middle strike, for a small net debit. It profits most if the underlying finishes at the middle strike.

collar.def: A position that holds shares, buys a put below their price and sells a call above it, often at no net cost, so that both the loss and the gain on the shares are capped.

CNDR index.def: Cboe's S&P 500 Iron Condor Index, a benchmark that tracks a strategy of selling SPX iron condors systematically. Its record, from a backtest starting in 1986 and live values since 2007, lags the S&P 500 by a wide margin.

probability of profit.def: The chance that a position finishes with any profit at all, however small. It says nothing about how large the losses are in the cases where it does not.

broken-wing butterfly.def: A butterfly spread with one wing wider than the other, often opened for a net credit, which removes the risk on one side and leaves a larger loss beyond the wider wing.

ladder.def: A three-strike option position that buys one option and sells two further out of the money at different strikes, collecting premium for a capped profit zone and leaving an uncapped loss on one side.

jade lizard.def: A position that sells an out-of-the-money put and an out-of-the-money call spread. When the total credit is at least the call spread's width it has no upside risk, and all its risk is below the put's strike.

ratio spread.def: A position that buys one option and sells two or more of the same type further out of the money. It profits from a modest move toward the sold strike and loses without limit on the side where it is net short.

broker call rate.def: The interest rate banks charge brokers for short-term loans that fund their customers' margin borrowing. Brokers set the margin rates they charge customers above it.

Treasury bill.def: A short-term debt security of the US government, maturing in a year or less and sold at a discount to its face value. Its yield is the usual benchmark for a short-term risk-free rate. Abbreviated T-bill.

federal funds rate.def: The interest rate at which US banks lend reserves to each other overnight, which the Federal Reserve targets as its main policy rate. Often shortened to fed funds.

conversion.def: An arbitrage that buys the underlying, sells a call and buys a put at one strike and expiry, locking in the strike at expiry. It profits only when the call is overpriced against the put by put-call parity.

reversal.def: The mirror image of a conversion: it shorts the underlying, buys a call and sells a put at one strike and expiry. It profits only when the call is underpriced against the put by put-call parity.
